messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Publisher
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Vulnerability: Being naked, Public Transport: Bus riding, Feeling Tired: Feeling very tired or exhausted
  Threat: Threat in Faces: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Karim

Karim was thirty-two when his brother Tariq was shot during a carjacking in East Oakland. The details arrived in fragments over the following hours—a parking garage at dusk, an argument that escalated, a weapon produced, Tariq's body found slumped in the driver's seat of his own car. Karim had not been there. He learned about it over the phone from a hospital social worker, and then again from police, and then again from his wife Leah, who had picked him up from work because she thought he should not drive. What made the trauma worse, in a way he could not fully articulate, was precisely that he had not witnessed it. His mind had filled the gaps with images his brother must have seen—the face of the person who shot him, the moment of recognition that this was real, the last thing Tariq felt. Karim's imagination had become the crime scene.

Two years had passed since that day, and Karim remained suspended in a state of hypervigilance that had calcified into the architecture of his daily life. He worked as a publisher in San Francisco, a job that had once involved travel to conferences and manuscript events, but he had gradually withdrawn from those obligations. His colleagues had stopped asking him to attend readings across the Bay; they understood, or thought they did, that he was simply grieving. What they did not see was the precise mechanism of his withdrawal. When Karim boarded a bus—and he had to, because driving alone had become intolerable—he positioned himself near the exit and studied every passenger with an intensity that exhausted him. He was looking for the shape of violence in a stranger's posture, the glint of intent in their eyes. He had come to believe that threat was readable if you looked hard enough, that the person who had murdered his brother had probably shown signs, had probably been legible to someone who knew how to look. Now Karim looked at everyone. On the 38 Geary heading into the city, he would scan faces, note the bulge of a jacket pocket, calculate which passengers might be carrying weapons. The act of riding the bus triggered an immediate flood of vigilance—his heart rate would climb, his jaw would tighten—and within moments the memories would arrive unbidden.

The memories came not as a coherent narrative but as shards. A parking garage. Fluorescent light. The sound of a voice raised in anger—Karim heard it now, internally, a phantom audio that played whenever his threat detection spiked. Then the image of Tariq's face, though Karim had never actually seen it that way, slack and final. Then the weapon, though again, he had not been there. These fragments did not arrange themselves into a story; they collided and separated and recombined, like pieces of a puzzle that had never belonged to the same box. And the more Karim scanned faces on public transport, the more he noticed potential weapons—the corner of something metallic in a backpack, the outline of an object he could not quite identify—the more intensely the memories would fragment and replay. He had come to understand that his vigilance was feeding the memories, but he could not stop because if he stopped looking, if he lowered his guard even once, he might miss the warning sign that would have saved his brother's life.

Leah had noticed the change first. He had always been a modest man, but now he could not undress in front of her without a creeping sense of exposure, of defenselessness. Being naked meant being unable to flee, unable to fight, unable to see an approaching threat. It meant being as vulnerable as Tariq must have been in that moment—caught, immobilized, at the mercy of someone else's violence. The feeling of exhaustion made it worse. When Karim was tired, his vigilance became even more rigid, more desperate. He would feel his attention fragmenting just when he needed it most, and the anxiety would spike—what if he missed something? What if he was too tired to notice the danger? And then the memories would come flooding back, the film playing on repeat: the garage, the voice, the weapon, Tariq's face. His threat detection would spike again, and he would find himself avoiding unfamiliar places entirely, unable to tolerate the unpredictability of an environment he could not fully assess. He had stopped attending his publisher's meetings in Oakland. He took the same routes on the same days, as if repetition and control could somehow prevent what had already happened. His marriage was strained. Leah had asked him, gently, to see someone. He had resisted for months, afraid that naming these patterns would make them real, would confirm what he already suspected: that he would never feel safe again, that he would never stop looking for the face of his brother's killer in every crowd, that the memories would never stop their relentless replay.

It was only when Leah told him she was considering leaving—that she could not bear to watch him disappear into this cage of his own making—that Karim finally made the call. He sat in the waiting room of the clinic, studying the faces of other patients, and wondered if anyone here understood what it meant to be haunted not by what you had witnessed, but by what you had imagined. He was thirty-four years old. He wanted to ride a bus without scanning for weapons. He wanted to know what it felt like to be naked without terror. He wanted the film to stop playing. Most of all, he wanted to stop looking for his brother's killer in the eyes of strangers, because he was beginning to suspect that the person he was most afraid of was himself—or rather, the version of himself that had been created by his own desperate need to understand something that could never be understood.
